analysis.one_liner: Guarantees managed-care patients emergency and specialist access, outside appeals, and clinical-trial coverage, while limiting lawsuits against insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 75 cosponsors, 74 of them Republicans, but was referred to three House committees and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill sets a federal floor of patient protections for people in employer-based managed care plans: emergency care without prior authorization, direct access to OB/GYN care, pediatricians as children's primary doctors, timely specialist access, continuity of care during transitions, independent outside review of denied claims, and coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials. In exchange, it limits patients' ability to sue their plans — pre-empting some state lawsuits and restricting class actions — and expands tax-advantaged medical savings accounts and association health plans. It was introduced as the Republican counterproposal to a broader bill that would have given patients a wider right to sue their plans; neither became law.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of people in employer-based managed care plans. They would gain guaranteed emergency coverage under a 'prudent layperson' standard with no extra charge for out-of-network emergency rooms, no referral requirement for OB/GYN care, the right to name a pediatrician as a child's primary doctor, timely access to specialists and out-of-network specialists at in-network cost when none is available, continued treatment from a doctor the plan drops during an active course of care, strict deadlines for claim decisions with independent external review of denials, disclosure of plan rules and physician payment methods, and coverage of routine patient costs in NIH- or FDA-approved clinical trials.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency services without prior authorization, whether or not the provider is in-network, with the patient liable only for in-network cost-sharing, under a prudent-layperson standard; emergency ambulance rides get the same treatment.
Plans cannot require a referral or authorization for a woman to see an OB/GYN in the network, and children may be assigned a pediatrician as their primary care provider.

Plans must provide timely coverage for specialist care; when no in-network specialist is available, out-of-network specialty care must cost the patient no more than in-network care. Patients with life-threatening or disabling conditions can keep seeing a dropped provider for up to 90 days, through pregnancy, or for the remainder of life in terminal illness.

Denied claims must follow strict timelines — 72 hours for expedited determinations, 24 hours for concurrent inpatient decisions — with internal appeals and then independent external review; a missed deadline counts as a denial. Plans must also disclose benefits, cost-sharing, provider directories, compensation methods, and appeal rights, with penalties up to $100 per person per day for failing to do so.

Patients with life-threatening or serious illnesses that standard treatment cannot help may not be denied participation in approved clinical trials, and the plan must cover routine patient costs in them.
Plan restrictions on what a doctor may tell a patient about care are null and void, and the bill expands Archer medical savings accounts and sets federal rules for association health plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health plans, insurers, and the employers behind them bear the compliance cost of disclosure, appeal deadlines, emergency and out-of-network coverage, and clinical-trial routine costs, which could feed into premiums. Patients could pay more for point-of-service (out-of-network) options, which plans are allowed to price higher, and plans with 26 or more employees only — not small employers — must even offer that option. Patients denied care also get weaker court recourse: the bill pre-empts some state lawsuits over benefit denials and limits class actions.

drawbacks.text: The bill pre-empts certain state causes of action over benefit denials and limits class-action litigation, so patients wronged by a plan have weaker recourse in court than under state law or the rival bipartisan proposal that would have created a broader right to sue.

Most protections apply only when the plan already covers the service in question — a plan can sidestep a mandate by dropping or limiting that benefit — and the point-of-service option carries a small-employer exemption and allows higher premiums and cost-sharing for going out of network.

The outside appeals process may carry a filing fee of up to $50 (waived for the poor, refunded if the denial is overturned), and expanding Archer medical savings accounts and association health plans is a tax-advantaged route that critics warned would pull healthier, higher-income enrollees out of broader risk pools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and specific: guaranteed emergency care, no gatekeeping for OB/GYN visits, appeal deadlines with real consequences, and clinical-trial coverage would matter to people fighting their plans over care. But the accountability core was deliberately narrower than the bipartisan bill pending at the same time — no broad right to sue, state lawsuits pre-empted, class actions restricted — and the access guarantees have coverage-conditioned edges and small-employer carve-outs. As a patient bill it was a moderate step; as a liability shield it gave plans and employers most of what they wanted.

outcome.mechanism: It went to three House committees and a health subcommittee, sat there for eighteen months, and died when the Congress ended in January 2003 without any committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2001 by Rep. Ernie Fletcher with 53 original cosponsors, all Republicans, and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees.
On July 6, 2001 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where no markup or vote ever followed.
The only later action in the record is sponsor introductory remarks on October 17, 2002; the bill never reached the House floor.
By the time the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, no version of a patients' bill of rights had become law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor health plans: no new federal patient protections, claim-deadline rules, disclosure mandates, or lawsuit exposure ever took effect. The patients whose protections were being debated in 2001 got nothing from this bill or its rivals.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 74 of 223 House Republicans and just 1 of 208 House Democrats cosponsored, while the rival bipartisan patients' bill of the same period drew sponsors from both parties.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill imposes concrete duties on plans — emergency coverage, appeal deadlines, disclosure with daily penalties, external review — but in trade it caps their courtroom exposure by pre-empting state suits and limiting class actions. That trade was the industry-preferred alternative to the broader right-to-sue bill before Congress the same year, and neither version passed.

Under ERISA, self-insured employers largely escape state court remedies; this bill keeps that shield while applying federal protection standards through their plans, so they get predictable federal rules without broad new liability.
The bill pre-empts certain state causes of action over benefit denials and limits class-action litigation, shrinking the malpractice-style route patients and their lawyers use against plans.

industries.industry: Trade associations and insurers offering association health plans
industries.note: Title VI creates a federal certification and operating framework for association health plans, letting small employers band together under federal rather than some state rules — a route critics said would skim healthier enrollees from state-regulated pools.

industries.industry: Banks and insurers selling Archer medical savings accounts
industries.note: The bill repeals the cap on the number of Archer MSAs and increases the deduction for contributions, enlarging a tax-advantaged product whose benefits concentrate among higher-income households who can fund the accounts.
